name: Anak
title: Ancestor of the Anakim, a giant people in Canaan
summary: As the eponymous ancestor of the Anakites, Anak gave his name to a feared people of unusually large warriors who controlled the mountainous regions of southern Canaan with Hebron (Kiriath-Arba) as their power center. His father Arba is described as the foremost among the Anakites, and the city of Hebron originally bore his name. The Anakites are counted in Scripture among the so-called giant peoples, together with the Rephaim and the Emim. When Moses sent twelve spies into Canaan, the mighty stature of Anak’s descendants became the decisive turning point: ten of the spies declared conquest impossible, and the resulting panic-driven rebellion against God led to the judgment of forty years of wandering in the wilderness (Num 13–14). Only Caleb and Joshua held fast to trust in God’s promise. Generations later, Joshua carried out a systematic campaign that drove the Anakites from the mountainous regions, and the aged Caleb fulfilled his personal calling by expelling three named descendants of Anak—Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai—from Hebron. Some Anakites survived in the Philistine coastal cities of Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod, a detail that links their history further to later biblical narrative. In the theological whole, the Anakites serve as a paradigmatic image of overwhelming opposition that can be overcome only through unwavering faith in God’s promises—a lesson fully expressed through the contrast between the people’s fear and Caleb’s steadfastness.

keyEvents.title: The Spies Discover the Anakim
keyEvents.description: When Moses sent twelve spies into the land of Canaan, they reported seeing descendants of Anak—giants who made the spies feel like grasshoppers by comparison. Hebron, where the Anakim lived, was especially highlighted.

keyEvents.title: The people's fear and rebellion
keyEvents.description: The terrifying size of the Anakites caused panic among the Israelites, who refused to enter the Promised Land. This rebellion led to God's judgment: an entire generation had to die in the wilderness during 40 years of wandering.

keyEvents.title: Caleb's faith regarding the Anakites
keyEvents.description: Caleb and Joshua were the only spies who trusted God's promise and insisted that Israel could defeat the Anakites. Caleb later asked for the hill country where the Anakites lived as his inheritance, relying on God's power.

keyEvents.title: Joshua destroys the Anakites from the hill countries
keyEvents.description: During the conquest of Canaan, Joshua led a comprehensive campaign against the Anakites in the hill countries—Hebron, Debir, and Anab—and wiped them out there. Only in the Philistine coastal cities of Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod did some survive.

keyEvents.title: Caleb captures Hebron and drives out the descendants of Anak
keyEvents.description: The now 85-year-old Caleb drove the three descendants of Anak—Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai—from Hebron, which was formerly called Kiriath-Arba after Arba, the father of Anak. This fulfilled the promise Caleb had received 45 years earlier.

keyEvents.title: Arba as the father of Anak and founder of Hebron
keyEvents.description: Arba, the father of Anak, is described as the greatest man among the Anakites. The city of Hebron was originally called Kiriath-Arba ('Arba's City') after him, which testifies to this family's dominant position in the hill country of southern Canaan.

versions.summary: Anak was the ancestor of the Anakites, a people of giants who lived in the land of Canaan, especially in the hill country around Hebron. The Anakites were feared for their great size and strength, and it was fear of them that caused the Israelites to refuse to enter the Promised Land after the report of the spies. They were later defeated by Joshua and Caleb during the conquest of Canaan.
versions.title: The ancestor of the Anakites
versions.reason: [minor] Anak likely lived before the conquest period. He was the ancestor of the Anakim, who were already established in Canaan when the spies arrived. An era such as 'patriarchs' or 'judges' could also be considered, but 'conquest' is acceptable since it is during this period that he is most frequently mentioned in the Bible.; [major] The role 'leader' is not well documented in the Bible. Anak is primarily described as an ancestor (forefather) of the Anakim. There is no biblical text describing him as a leader in a political or military sense. The role should be changed to something like 'ancestor' or 'eponym'.; [minor] Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai are described in the Bible as 'Anak's children/descendants' (Num 13:22; Josh 15:14), but the Hebrew word 'yelide' can also mean 'descendants' in a broader sense, not necessarily direct sons. The profile is still reasonable.; [minor] The summary is good, but could clarify that Anak himself was not necessarily a historical individual—the name may also function as an eponym (a name representing the entire people group). This is an important linguistic and theological nuance.; [major] There are no footnotes that shed light on the historical, archaeological, linguistic and theological aspects of Anak and the Anakim. Footnotes should be added covering etymology, possible archaeological connections and theological significance.; [minor] The event 'Arba as Anak's father and founder of Hebron' concerns Arba more than Anak. It is acceptable as context but may be considered secondary for the Anak profile.

versions.title: Ancestor of the Anakim, a giant people in Canaan
versions.reason: [minor] Anak lived before the conquest of Canaan – he belongs to an earlier generation (perhaps the patriarchal or pre-conquest era). 'Conquest' can be defended because Anak is first mentioned in a conquest context, but strictly speaking, he was an older figure. Nevertheless, 'conquest' is retained since it is difficult to place him precisely.; [major] Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai are described in the Bible as descendants/sons of Anak, but it is unclear whether they were direct sons or more distant descendants. The biblical text (Num 13:22; Josh 15:14; Judg 1:20) says 'Anak's children/descendants' – they lived in Joshua's time, potentially hundreds of years after Anak himself. It should be clarified in the summary that these are likely clan designations rather than direct sons.; [minor] The summary is thorough and good, but resembles the previous version (version 1) very closely. It should be rephrased somewhat to provide fresh wording and avoid repetition. Something could also be added about the connection with the Rephaim (Deut 2:10-11).; [minor] The link between the Anakim and Goliath is an interesting speculation, but calling the source 'rabbinic' is somewhat misleading – this is a theory from modern biblical scholars. 'Theological' or 'historical' would have been more precise.; [minor] This footnote deals more with historical and linguistic connections among various giant peoples than with theology. The source label 'theological' could have been 'historical' or 'linguistic'.; [minor] Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai are referred to as 'the three descendants of Anak'. 'Descendants' is better than 'sons' given the chronological distance, but it should be used consistently throughout the profile.

versions.summary: Anak was the eponymous ancestor of the Anakites, a feared people of giants who dominated the mountainous regions of southern Canaan, with Hebron (Kiriath-Arba) as their center. The Bible mentions the Anakites together with the Rephaites and Emim as peoples of extraordinary physical size. When Moses sent spies into Canaan, the towering figures of the Anakites became the very symbol of impossible odds – ten out of twelve spies believed it was impossible to defeat them, and the people's fear triggered a rebellion that resulted in 40 years of wandering in the wilderness (Num 13–14). Anak's father Arba is described as the greatest among the Anakites, and the city of Hebron bore his name. Despite the overwhelming fear they inspired, the Anakites were defeated by Joshua during the conquest of Canaan, and the elderly Caleb completed the personal mission of driving out Anak's descendants – Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai – from Hebron. Some Anakites survived in the Philistine coastal cities of Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod. In the biblical narrative, the Anakites stand as a theological example of overwhelming obstacles that can only be overcome through unwavering trust in God's promises and power.
versions.title: Ancestor of the Anakim, a giant people in Canaan
versions.reason: [major] Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai are described in the Bible as descendants of Anak (benei ha-'Anaq), but they are not necessarily his direct sons. Joshua 15:14 and Judges 1:20 refer to them as "the three sons of Anak," yet given that they lived during Joshua's time (many generations after Anak himself), they are more likely descendants than immediate children. This should be reflected more clearly, even though the biblical text uses "sons" (which often means descendants in Hebrew).; [minor] Anak himself probably lived before the conquest period. He was a patriarch from an earlier era, while his descendants encountered the Israelites during the conquest. Still, "conquest" is appropriate since it is during this period that Anak and his people are most relevant in the biblical narrative. "Patriarchs" or "judges" could have been alternatives, but conquest covers the main part of the story.; [minor] The summary is very good and detailed, but this is now the third version and should differ more from the two earlier versions, both of which began with "Anak was the father of the Anakites." A somewhat different introduction would strengthen the profile.; [minor] The role "eponym" is correct but could be supplemented with a role such as "founder of the people group" or similar to provide more context about his function in the biblical narrative.

footnotes.text: The name 'Anak' (Hebrew: עֲנָק, 'Anaq') likely means 'long neck' or 'necklace/neck ring.' The root ענק can point to physical size or to a necklace/jewel. In Proverbs 1:9, the related word עֲנָק is used for a necklace around the neck. The name functions both as a personal name and as an eponym for the entire people group of the Anakites (benei ha-'Anaq, 'sons of Anak').

The Anakites have been attempted to be identified with various historical peoples. Egyptian execration texts from the 19th–18th centuries BCE mention rulers in Canaanite cities that may be linked to the Hebron area. Some scholars have also pointed to possible connections with the Philistine sea-people traditions, but secure identifications are lacking.

Hebron (Kiriath-Arba) is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, with settlement traces dating back to the Bronze Age. Archaeological excavations at Tel Rumeida (ancient Hebron) have uncovered fortifications from the Middle Bronze Age that testify to a significant city fortress, possibly the one controlled by the Anakites.

In Deuteronomy 2:10–11, the Anakites are compared with the Rephaites and Emim, and in Deuteronomy 2:20–21, the Zamzummim are also mentioned. These connections show that traditions about peoples of unusually large size were widespread in the ancient Near East and were not limited to a single people group or region.

According to Josh 11:22, some Anakites survived in the Philistine cities of Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod. Several scholars have speculated whether the giant Goliath from Gath (1 Sam 17) may have been a descendant of these remaining Anakites, which would create a narrative bridge from Joshua's incomplete conquest to David's famous battle.

Theologically, the Anakites serve as a powerful symbol in the biblical story: they represent seemingly insurmountable obstacles that can only be overcome through faith in God. The contrast between the ten fearful spies and Caleb's faith (Num 13–14) is a recurring theme in Jewish and Christian preaching about the power of faith over fear.

The Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) renders the Anakites with various terms, including γίγαντες (gigantes, 'giants'), the same word used for the Nephilim in Gen 6:4. This translational approach has helped link the Anakites closely to the broader tradition of prehistoric giants in biblical and extrabiblical texts.

In rabbinic sources (including Bavli Sota 34b), the enormous size of the Anakites is elaborated with colorful details. According to one tradition, Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai were so large that the sun was hidden by their necks. Such midrashic texts emphasize the hyperbolic fear the spies must have felt and reinforce the theological point about faith versus fear.
